title: Uddhava Delivers Krishna's Message and the Gopis Reply
story:
A real messenger had come at last. For months the women of Vrindavan had poured their grief into the empty air; they had even pleaded with a bee, mistaking it for a courier from Mathura. Now a man stood before them who had actually travelled from Krishna, carrying words from his own mouth. His name was Uddhava, and the verses say he had been sent for this one purpose — to bring the women of Vraja some word from the friend who had left them.

Uddhava was Krishna's friend and counsellor, a man of learning and restraint, and the verses make a point of what he did first. Before he spoke a single word of the message, he praised the gopis. Through gifts, vows, austerities, sacrifice, study and self-control, he told them, they had offered up sons, husbands, homes and their own bodies to a single love, and that love had made them peerless — no one on earth had done what they had done. Only then, having honored them, did he speak Krishna's words.

The message was not an apology, and it was not a promise to return. Krishna asked them to see that he had never truly been far from them at all. As ether and air, fire, water and earth pervade every living being, so he pervaded all things; he was the one who creates, preserves and destroys by his own self alone, the self made of pure knowledge, untouched by the world's qualities. There was nothing outside him to be lost. A beloved who is far away, he said, remains close in the mind of the one who loves; so let them fix their minds wholly on him, and they would soon attain him. This, he said, was the whole conclusion of the scriptures, of yoga and of the wise. And then, almost a memory spoken aloud: it was he who had played with them at night in this very forest of Vraja.

The gopis did not accept it, and they did not refuse it. They answered with a grief so steady it had become its own kind of truth.

Does he remember us? they asked. Does Govinda, who understands every shade of love, remember the nights when the moon hung bright over Vrindavan, the groves white with jasmine and kunda blossom, and he danced among us, his ankle-bells ringing, while we praised him with our songs? Will the Dasarha ever come back here, scorched by a sorrow of his own making? He has won a kingdom now and slain his enemies; why would he return to us, women of the forest? What are we, who live in the woods, to that great soul? And then the heart of it, the question behind every other question: who could bear to give up the memory of him? These rivers, these hills and forest paths, these cows, the sound of the flute — everything in this place calls back the son of Nanda, again and again. O lord, O lord of Rama, O lord of Vraja, remover of sorrows.

So the exchange ended not in comfort but in a strange completion. Krishna had asked them to fix their minds on him; they answered that they could not do otherwise — that the world around them would not let them forget, and that forgetting was the one thing their love could not manage. What he had called a path to union, they had already been walking, without choosing it, from the day he left. Uddhava, who had come to teach them, stood silent, and something in the learned man began to turn.
reflection: The gopis cannot be consoled by argument because what they carry is not ignorance but love. Krishna asks for a mind fixed wholly on him, and their reply — that rivers, hills and a flute will not let them forget — is that very fixing, already accomplished. Their longing is the union he describes.
next_story_tease: But their reply undid the messenger, and Uddhava would soon wish to trade his learning for a place in the dust of their feet.
hero_scene: Uddhava standing before the gopis in a Vrindavan grove at dusk, the women gathered around him, their faces lifted as they answer that every river, hill and the sound of the flute will not let them forget Krishna.
